summary: German chooses its preposition by what kind of place it is and by whether you are there, going there or coming from there. WHERE (Wo?): in for inside a building, room, town or country (in der Schule, im Büro, in Berlin); an for an edge or a side (am Bahnhof, am Fenster, an der Uni); bei for a person, a doctor, a firm (bei meiner Oma, beim Arzt, bei der Arbeit); zu Hause = at home. WHERE TO (Wohin?): zu for a person or a place you go to for its purpose (zum Arzt, zur Schule, zur Post); nach for cities and countries without an article and for home (nach Athen, nach Griechenland, nach Hause); in + accusative for going inside (ins Café, in die Stadt). FROM (Woher?): aus = out of, origin (aus Griechenland, aus dem Haus); von = from a person or a starting point, and “of” (von meiner Mutter, von der Arbeit, vom Markt). WITH: mit (Tee mit Milch, mit meinem Bruder). WITHOUT: ohne. FOR: für. ABOUT: über (ein Buch über die Stadt). Preposition and article often merge into one word: im, ins, am, ans, zum, zur, beim, vom – the merged form is the normal one (im Park, not *in dem Park). Every preposition also fixes the case of the noun after it (fn.case): aus, bei, mit, nach, von, zu + dative; für, ohne + accusative; in and an + dative for “where”, accusative for “where to”.

blocks.title: bei is never “to”
blocks.text: Ich bin bei meiner Mutter (I am at my mother’s). Going there: Ich gehe zu meiner Mutter – not *bei meiner Mutter gehen.

blocks.title: aus or von?
blocks.text: Where you are from is aus: Ich bin aus Griechenland. von is a starting point or a person: Ich komme von der Arbeit. Das Buch ist von Anna.

blocks.title: zu Hause / nach Hause
blocks.text: zu Hause = at home (where), nach Hause = home (where to).

blocks.title: Open places take auf
blocks.text: A market, a square or the street is not “in”: auf dem Markt, auf dem Platz, auf der Straße (S12).

askYourself: Am I somewhere (Wo?), going somewhere (Wohin?) or coming from somewhere (Woher?)?
Where: is it inside (in), at an edge or a point like a station or a university (an), at a person’s or a firm’s place (bei) – or at home (zu Hause)?
Where to: a person or a place I visit for its purpose (zu), a city or country without article or home (nach), or into a building or room (in + accusative)?
From: origin or out of (aus), or a starting point / a person (von)?
Can the article merge (im, ins, am, ans, zum, zur, beim, vom)? Then use the merged form.
Which case does the preposition need? (aus, bei, mit, nach, von, zu → dative; für, ohne → accusative).
steps: Decide where / where to / where from.
Choose the preposition for the kind of place.
Give the article the case the preposition needs; merge it if possible.

traps: One idea, several words: in der Schule (where), zur Schule (where to), am Bahnhof, beim Arzt, zu Hause.
Not *bei Hause / *in Hause: zu Hause (where), nach Hause (where to).
Cities and countries without article take nach for “to” (nach Berlin), countries with article take in + accusative (in die Türkei).
Origin is aus, not von: Ich bin aus Athen.
bei is only for “at”, never for movement.
Use the merged form: im Park, zum Arzt, zur Post – in dem Park sounds like “in that park”.
über meaning “about” takes the accusative: über die Stadt (not *über der Stadt).

quiz.why: Where → zu Hause; where to → nach Hause.

quiz.q: Mein Opa ist ___ Arzt. (at the doctor’s)
quiz.why: At a person’s / doctor’s place = bei (bei dem → beim).
Going to a place you visit = zu (zu dem → zum).

quiz.q: Das ist ein Buch ___ die Stadt. (about)

quiz.why: Where: in der Schule; where to: zur Schule.
German needs in / an / bei (where) and zu / nach / in (where to).

seeAlso.note: Arabic fī (in), ilā (to), min (from), maʿa (with), bidūn (without), li- (for), ʿan (about) – every noun after them is in the genitive.
Hebrew be- (in, at), le- (to), mi- (from) are written joined to the noun; im (with), bli (without), bishvil (for), al (about) are separate words.
Chinese uses verbs as prepositions (coverbs): 在 (at), 从 (from), 跟 (with), 给 (for) – no cases and no merged forms.
Each preposition fixes the case: dative after aus, bei, mit, nach, von, zu; accusative after für, ohne.

notes.text: σε alone covers in, at and to: στο σχολείο is in der Schule (where) and zur Schule (where to); German also needs am Bahnhof, beim Arzt, zu Hause. από covers both aus (origin: aus Griechenland) and von (a starting point: von der Arbeit). With με German needs the dative: mit meinem Bruder.
в / на + case for “where” and “where to” work like in / an + case, and дома / домой split exactly as zu Hause / nach Hause. из / от match aus / von.
en covers in, at and on (en la escuela, en la mesa) and a covers “to”; German splits by place and direction: in der Schule, zur Schule, am Bahnhof, nach Madrid.
at my mother’s is bei meiner Mutter, to my mother is zu meiner Mutter; at home – zu Hause, home – nach Hause. German merges preposition and article: im, am, zum, zur.
chez ma mère is both bei meiner Mutter (where) and zu meiner Mutter (where to); German splits them. à Paris is in Paris or nach Paris.
Hindi postpositions follow the noun (ghar mẽ, ghar se, ghar ko); German prepositions precede it and fix its case: im Haus, aus dem Haus.
Persian prepositions come first as in German (dar xāne, be xāne, az xāne); but be covers every “to”, where German chooses nach, zu or in.
Marathi puts the place relation at the end of the noun (gharāt – in the house, gharī – at home / home, gharūn – from the house); German puts a preposition before it.
fī, ilā, min, maʿa all take the genitive; German prepositions each fix their own case (mit + dative, für + accusative). ʿinda (at someone’s) is bei.
be-, le-, mi- are prefixes on the noun; German has separate words, which merge with the article (im, zum, vom). etsel (at someone’s place) is bei: bei meiner Mutter.
Turkish uses case suffixes: evde (zu Hause), eve (nach Hause), evden (von zu Hause), okulda (in der Schule), okula (zur Schule). German puts a preposition before the noun and changes the article.
Japanese particles follow the noun (gakkō ni / de / e / kara); German prepositions precede it, and the choice depends on the kind of place too.
Korean particles follow the noun (hakgyo-e, hakgyo-eseo); German prepositions come first and choose by place and direction.
Finnish local cases split where / where to / where from just as German does (talossa – taloon – talosta: im Haus – ins Haus – aus dem Haus); German uses prepositions instead of endings.
Hungarian suffixes split where / where to / where from (házban – házba – házból), the same three questions as Wo? / Wohin? / Woher?; German uses prepositions.
Swahili -ni makes a place (nyumbani – at home and home; shuleni – at school and to school); German splits the two: zu Hause / nach Hause, in der Schule / zur Schule.
在 + place for “where”, 去 + place for “where to”, 从 for “from”; in German the preposition and the case of the article change with the direction: in der Schule, in die Schule.
ở (at), đến (to), từ (from) never change the noun; German prepositions change the article’s case.
Inuktitut case endings split where / where to / where from (iglumi – iglumut – iglumit), the same three questions as Wo? / Wohin? / Woher?; German uses prepositions instead.
